source_read: PDF (scan), Science 190: 912-914, all three pages read on the rendered page at 150 dpi; Tables 1 and 2, note 4, Figure 1 and the discussion paragraphs checked on 300- and 600-dpi crops; the text layer (tables scrambled) used only to locate passages

claims.overstatement: The Kandel sentences do not overstate the source; the claim's overall verdict of insufficient evidence fits this unadjusted panel. Three wording points. (1) 'the abstract calls cannabis a crucial step ..., while the text says a drug does not invariably lead to the next': the body also calls marijuana a crucial step and a crucial stage (p. 913, left column). The tension is between those statements and the qualifications on p. 914, not between abstract and text. Suggested: 'the paper calls cannabis a crucial step (abstract and p. 913) but also says ...'. (2) 'These percentages were not adjusted for anything': they were not adjusted for other characteristics, but they are survey-weighted, for selection probabilities and school response, and the panel was reweighted to reproduce the time-1 marijuana frequency (note 4). 'Not adjusted for other characteristics' would be exact. (3) The four destinations in Table 1 (12 + 9 + 2 + 2) sum to 25 percentage points; the text and Figure 1 give 26%, presumably from unrounded cells. Harmless, but the claim's breakdown and its total come from different places.
claims.note: All numbers from this source checked on the rendered pages. Sample: random sample of New York State public secondary school students in 18 schools, self-administered classroom questionnaires in fall 1971 and spring 1972 (5-6 months), N = 5,468 matched; usable questionnaires 8,206 at time 1 and 7,250 at time 2, so 5,468/8,206 = 66.6% (printed: 66 percent matched by self-generated codes); unmatched cases had a higher proportion of drug users (note 4). Seniors re-contacted 5-9 months after graduation (N = 985; 69% response; 60% matched), winter 1972-1973. Table 1 (cannabis at T1, N = 558): interval use legal only 19, cannabis 55 + 1 (error) = 56, pills 9 + 3 = 12 (the footnote's own example), psychedelics 5 + 4 = 9, cocaine 0 + 2 = 2, heroin 1 + 1 = 2. Legal only at T1 (N = 2,911): pills 2 + 1 error, psychedelics 1 error = 4%. None at T1 (N = 482): 1% error at pills. Table 2: cannabis in the interval 27% among current users of cigarettes, liquor and beer/wine (N >= 342) vs 2% among those who had never used any (N >= 467). The seniors' cohort: 16% moved from marijuana to other illicit drugs (p. 913). Other context: only about 2-3% of legal-only users went to other illicit drugs without cannabis (p. 913; the scan prints '2 c 3'); the Table 1 column Ns sum to 4,588, not 5,468, without explanation; the author says the sequences were similar across grades, sexes, family education and race, with data not presented (p. 914).

anchors.extracted: 27% of students who smoke and drink start marijuana within 5-6 months vs 2% of those who used no legal drug; 26% of students using marijuana progress to LSD, amphetamines or heroin vs 1% of non-users and 4% of legal-only users; marijuana called a crucial step towards other illicit drugs; sequence seen in each high-school year and the year after graduation.

Two-phase random sample representative of New York State public secondary school students, self-administered classroom questionnaires in fall and spring of one school year, 5-6 months apart (N = 5,468); seniors from the same 18 schools re-contacted 5-9 months after graduation (N = 985); ever and past-month use of 14 substances, and use during the interval.

Usable questionnaires from 8,206 students at time 1 and 7,250 at time 2; 66% of fall students matched to themselves in spring by self-generated codes (60% of seniors after graduation; graduate follow-up response 69%). Unmatched cases included more drug users; the panel was weighted to reproduce the time-1 marijuana frequency of the full cross-sectional sample.

Students at the cannabis step in fall 1971 (N = 558), highest step used fall 1971 to spring 1972: legal only 19%, cannabis 55% (+1% error), pills 9% (+3% error; 12% in all, as the footnote states), psychedelics 5% (+4%), cocaine 2% (error), heroin 1% (+1%). Legal-only at T1 (N = 2,911): none 10%, legal 79%, cannabis 7%, pills 2% plus errors at pills 1% and psychedelics 1%. None at T1 (N = 482): none 62%, legal 36%, cannabis 1%, error at pills 1%. Percentages only; no adjustment.

The author calls marijuana a crucial step and a crucial stage before other illicit drugs; only about 2-3% of legal-drug users in each cohort went to other illicit drugs without first trying marijuana; progression from marijuana to other illicit drugs: 26% over 5-6 months in high school, 16% among graduated seniors.

anchors.locator: Table 2, T1 to T2 panel, Cannabis row
anchors.extracted: Among exclusive legal-drug users classified by current use at T1, cannabis use in the interval: 27% of current users of cigarettes, liquor and beer/wine (N >= 342), 16% of cigarettes only (N >= 70) and of cigarettes + beer/wine (N >= 356), 11% of liquor + beer/wine (N >= 429), 4% of beer/wine only (N >= 731), 5% not current (N >= 694), vs 2% of those who never used any (N >= 467).
Stage model, fall 1971 to spring 1972, ages 14-18: non-use to beer/wine .28; to marijuana .16 (hard liquor), .27 (both), .11 (cigarettes); marijuana to other illicit drugs .26.

A particular drug does not invariably lead to drugs higher in the sequence; many youths stop at a stage or regress; the stages are probably culturally determined, which only comparative and cross-cultural studies can settle.

Because each stage is cumulative, comparisons of users with non-users of a drug should be made among those who have already reached the preceding stage; otherwise traits attributed to users of that drug may belong to involvement at the preceding level.

key_findings.correction: Could add the first weighting in note 4: each wave weighted for the selection probabilities of schools and homerooms and for school response rates, besides the panel's reweighting to the time-1 marihuana frequency.
The 'only 2 or 3 percent' is printed as '2 c 3' in the scan (p. 913, left column), evidently a print defect.
Same reading and sum (25) in my blind extraction; interval reproduced (22-30%).
Intervals reproduced (27% of 342: 22-32%; 2% of 467: 1-3%); risk ratio 13.5.

Values match my 300-dpi reading. On the note: the figure is not a straight copy of Table 2 elsewhere either (beer/wine to cigarettes .08 vs 14%, non-use to beer/wine .28 vs 30%), because several starters were placed in order by assumption (legend; note 9). But .21 and .68 match Table 2 exactly and .16/.11 are an exact swap of 16/11, so 'appear transposed' is a fair, appropriately hedged reading.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high for the causal (gateway) question; confounding very high and selection high are right. As a description of the order of first use the panel is well sampled, as the reasoning says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One correction to the 'claimed' text: the running text is not only cautious. The body also calls marihuana a crucial step in the induction into illicit drug use, and a crucial stage before other illicit drugs (p. 913, left column, 8th paragraph). The causal-sounding wording and the caveats on p. 914 sit side by side in the body, not only abstract against text.
